title: Sama Cares for His Blind Parents
text:
In the forest near the Migasammata river lived two ascetics, husband and wife, with their only son, Sama. When Sama was still a boy, his parents were caught in a rainstorm and took shelter under a tree on top of an anthill. Water dripping from their bodies fell on a snake below, and its angry breath blinded them both.

From then on Sama looked after them completely. He fetched water and fruit, cleaned their hut, and stretched ropes between the hut and the river so that his parents could find their way. He was so gentle that the deer of the forest walked with him.

One day, as he filled his water jar, Piliyakkha, the king of Benares, out hunting, shot him with a poisoned arrow. As he lay dying, Sama's only concern was for his parents: who would care for them now? Stricken with remorse, the king went to the hut himself, told them what had happened, and promised to serve them as their son had.

The parents asked to be led to Sama's body. There they made a solemn act of truth, declaring his goodness to his parents. A goddess who had loved Sama in an earlier life added her own. The poison left him, Sama rose alive, and his parents' sight was restored.
lesson: Caring for aging parents is not a burden to hide but one of the most honorable things a person can do. Steady, daily care matters more than grand gestures.
people: Sama, his blind parents Dukulaka and Parika, King Piliyakkha
source: Jataka 540 (Sama Jataka, also called Suvannasama Jataka)
caveat: The collection was written down centuries after the Buddha, and the dating of individual tales is uncertain.
